## Overview

This blog focuses on the ["Parsing Inputs"](https://www.fuzzingbook.org/html/Parser.html) chapter of [The
Fuzzing Book](https://www.fuzzingbook.org/).

### Parsing Inputs

We have seen how grammars can be used to generate strings from a language. They
can also be used to break strings down to tell the parts of grammar they were
made from. A derivation tree would show a broken down string and its
hierarchical organization. You can use the derivation tree to recreate the
string, or you can swap put branches to create new strings. This is how parsing
can be used for fuzzing; get the parts of a valid input by parsing, and make a
few changes, while following the grammar, and you'll have new valid inputs to
use.

### Why Parsing for Fuzzing?

The book provides an example where parsing inputs for fuzzing could be useful. A
program takes in a CSV file of vehicle details and processes each line, behaving
differently with a van versus a car. Using a grammar for generating comma
separated values, 1000 inputs are created. None of them work, however, as the
vehicle types `car` and `van` aren't included. The grammar is updated to include
`car` and `van` as options, but many invalid inputs are still generated, having
either the wrong amount of comma separated values or incorrect types of one or
more of the values. The book suggests that instead the solution could be to get
the "template" for valid inputs by parsing valid samples and using them for
fuzzing.

```python
def process_van(year, company, model):
    res = ["We have a %s %s van from %s vintage." % (company, model, year)]
    iyear = int(year)
    if iyear > 2010:
        res.append("It is a recent model!")
    else:
        res.append("It is an old but reliable model!")
    return res
```

```python
def process_car(year, company, model):
    res = ["We have a %s %s car from %s vintage." % (company, model, year)]
    iyear = int(year)
    if iyear > 2016:
        res.append("It is a recent model!")
    else:
        res.append("It is an old but reliable model!")
    return res
```

### Using a Parser

A parser is "the part of a program that processes (structured) input". It takes
in an input string and outputs a derivation tree. Current parsers usually
require two steps: initialize the parser and give it some input to parse.

### An Ad Hoc Parser

The book creates a simple parser for demonstration. It takes the input and
breaks it down by line into records, and then by comma separated
value.`Display_tree()` is used to show a visual of an example derivation tree.
More complicated examples are then given, such as handling commas in quoted
values and handling embedded quotes. More and more changes would need to be made
to this parser, and it would be difficult to ensure you've gotten everything.
This is where formal parsers come in. Rather than trying to figure out every
parsing rule needed on your own, a formal parser is created directly from a
formal grammar (this includes context-free grammars).

```python
def simple_parse_csv(mystring: str) -> DerivationTree:
    children: List[DerivationTree] = []
    tree = (START_SYMBOL, children)
    for i, line in enumerate(mystring.split('\n')):
        children.append(("record %d" % i, [(cell, [])
                                           for cell in line.split(',')]))
    return tree
```

### Grammars in Parsing

#### Grammars and Derivation Trees

A grammar is "a set of rules that explain how the start symbol can be expanded.
Each rule has a name, also called a nonterminal, and a set of alternative
choices in how the nonterminal can be expanded." An example: `<expr>:
[<expr>+<expr>, <expr>-<expr>, <integer>]` It tells how the nonterminal `<expr>`
might be expanded. `<expr>` has three "alternative expansions", one of them
being `<expr>+<expr>` which can be broken down into three "symbols": `<expr>`,
`+`, and `<expr>`. Notice that a symbol can be nonterminal or terminal. From
this grammar, an input string can be made. For example, `"1+2"`. This input can
be parsed into a derivation tree. At the top of the tree is the `<start>`
symbol. All expansions made are shown until all terminals are reached.

#### Recursion

Using a nonterminal in its own definition, like with `<expr>`, is called
recursion. There are two types of recursion: left recursion and right recursion.
Some definitions:

- **Left Recursion**: when the left-most symbol of any expansion is the
nonterminal itself
- **Right Recursion**: when the right-most symbol of any expansion is the
nonterminal itself
- **Direct Recursion**: The symbol that causes left or right recursion is doing
so as one of the expansions of the nonterminal
- **Indirect Recursion**: The symbol that causes left or right recursion is
doing so as the expansion of another nonterminal that was reached from
expansions that trace back to the original nonterminal
- **Ambiguity**: When parsing an input to create a derivation tree, ambiguous
grammar may lead to multiple possible derivation trees

### A Parser Class

The Fuzzing Book describes two approaches for parsing:

- **Lexer**: Lexing breaks its source down into its smallest meaningful parts. Then,
these "parts," or "tokens," are fed to the parser to be organized into a
derivation tree.

- **Tree Pruner**: Use "a grammar that incorporates complete details of the syntax."
After parsing, "prune" the tree by replacing nodes that correspond to tokens
with their corresponding strings as leaf nodes.

The parser class the book defines uses the Tree Pruner option, and includes a
`parse` method which returns a list of derivation trees if the parse was
successful.

### Parsing Expression Grammars

A Parsing Expression Grammar (PEG) is a type of formal grammar that specifies
the sequence of steps to take to parse a given string. Both PEGs and
Context-Free Grammars use nonterminals and corresponding alternatives
representing how to match each. PEGs, however, use *ordered choice* and will
stop at the first match that succeeds. One technique for parsing PEGs is Packrat
parsing, which is so named because it caches results to avoid recomputation.

```python
PEG1 = {
    '<start>': ['a', 'b']
}
```

```python
PEG2 = {
    '<start>': ['ab', 'abc']
}
```

### Parsing Context-Free Grammars

#### Problems with PEG

Working with PEGs can be simple and intuitive with simple parser like packrat
parsers, but they don't easily cross over with Context-Free Grammars, which is
what the book has been using. It is not easy to translate from PEG to CFG, so
the book looks at a new type of parser.

#### The Earley Parser

Earley parsers are able to parse any arbitrary context-free grammar. It uses
chart parsing which is where it stores partial parses in tables to avoid any
backtracking. The book goes into detail about implementing an Earley parser.

### Lessons Learned

- Grammars can be used to generate derivation trees for a given string.
- PEGs are intuitive, and easy to implement, but require care to write.
- Earley Parsers can parse arbitrary Context Free Grammars.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" title="Open-Source Tool for Software Engineers" collapse="false"}

Our tool is [ParseBench](https://github.com/katie-sol/ParseBench), a benchmark that compares PEG and Earley parsers on speed, growth rate, and which strings each one accepts.

:::
